svg.aria-label: Diagram: how AWS Resource Explorer separates indexes from views, and where the access boundary actually sits. An index is the collection of information maintained by Resource Explorer about all of the AWS resources in one AWS Region in an AWS account. There are three index types: a Resource Explorer-owned index which exists in every AWS Region, is managed by the service, cannot be deleted or modified by users and returns immediate partial results; a user-owned local index which returns complete results with automatic updates; and an aggregator index, of which there can be only one in an AWS account, which receives a replica of every other user-owned index and is the only way to get account-wide search results. The structural rule between the two layers is that users cannot directly query the index and must always query using a view, stated on both the concepts page and the views page, and the index ARN can be used only in permission policies to grant access to operations that interact directly with the index, not as a search handle. There are three view types. User views can be modified and deleted by the user but have no access to config and relationship data. Managed views and service views cannot be modified by the user and do have access to config and relationship data, so AWS-owned views reach a tier of the inventory that a customer's own views cannot. Service views are automatically available to authorized callers without setup as a global resource and can be enumerated with the ListServiceViews API action. The central finding is that two true statements sit side by side. AWS states that views are the method the administrator can use to control access to the information about resources in an AWS account, and results from queries made with a view are always automatically filtered to include only those resources that match the view's criteria. AWS also states that if the AWS managed policy named AWSResourceExplorerReadOnlyAccess is used with principals, it grants them the ability to search using any view in the account. Together these mean a view restricts what it returns but does nothing about which views a principal may call, so a narrow filtered view confines nobody; it only adds an option beside every other view in the Region, including a default view which the documentation states does not have any filters. The real restriction is an IAM act on the view ARN: a principal must have Allow access to both the resource-explorer-2 GetView and resource-explorer-2 Search operations on the view's ARN, and a custom policy can restrict access to a single view or a subset by specifying the ARN of each view in the Resource element of the policy statement. Three constraints follow. First, scale: the default and maximum number of views in an AWS Region is ten and the quotas cannot be increased, Search is capped at five operations per second and non-Search at three, and views do not travel because they are stored per-Region, a view can access only the index in its own Region, only a view that exists in a Region can be that Region's default view, and there is no copy view operation. Second, absence is not denial: if no user-owned view exists in a Region, Resource Explorer automatically falls back to a Resource Explorer-owned view so that search remains available, those fallback views cannot be modified or deleted and do not include resource tags in search results, and automatic index creation occurs when a user holding at minimum the AWSResourceExplorerReadOnlyAccess managed policy performs a first search in a Region that has no user index, creating a default view with no filters. Third, two console search boxes disagree: Unified Search automatically inserts a wildcard character operator at the end of the first keyword in the string, while the Query text box on the Resource search page in the Resource Explorer console does not automatically append a wildcard, so the same string returns different result sets in the two places. Resource Explorer also deliberately excludes resource types whose inclusion would expose customer data, so Amazon S3 objects contained within a bucket, Amazon DynamoDB table items and DynamoDB attribute values are never returned in search results. The recommended audit is to find every principal holding the read-only managed policy or Search on all resources, list the Regions that have acquired a user-owned index against the Regions you intended to use, and call ListServiceViews to see which AWS-owned views exist.
svg.title: The filter and the grant are two different mechanisms, and only one of them is a boundary
svg.text: Every query goes through a view. No policy makes a view the only one you can use.
AWS Resource Explorer — the filtering is enforced by the service; the restriction is not, and is not here.
THE INDEX — three types, one Region each
Resource Explorer-owned · every Region · partial results
User-owned (local) · per Region · complete results
Aggregator · ONE per acct · replica of all
The index ARN is usable “only in permission policies” — it is
not a search handle. “Users can't directly query the index.”
Not indexed, ever: S3 objects, DynamoDB items and attribute values.
THE VIEW — the only way in
User views · you own · config/relationship data: NO
Managed views · AWS owns · config/relationship data: YES
Service views · AWS owns · config/relationship data: YES
Results are “always automatically filtered” to the view's
criteria. That part works exactly as advertised.
AWS-owned views see a tier your own views cannot. ListServiceViews.
Two sentences on the same documentation page. Both true. Read together, they are the whole post.
“Views are the method the administrator can use to control access to the information about resources
in your AWS account.”
“If you use the AWS managed policy named AWSResourceExplorerReadOnlyAccess with your principals,
it grants them the ability to search using any view in the account.”
A filtered view removes nothing from anyone. It adds an option beside a default view that “doesn't have any filters”.
The boundary is one line in an IAM policy, in a different console, that nothing reminds you to write
Allow resource-explorer-2:GetView + resource-explorer-2:Search on arn:aws:resource-explorer-2:...:view/Name/UUID
1 · Ten views. Not raisable.
Default 10, maximum 10, per Region.
“You cannot increase the quotas”.
Search: 5/sec. Non-search: 3/sec.
Per-Region, and “no copy view
operation” — so no replication.
2 · Absence is not a denial.
No view? A fallback view is used,
and it cannot be deleted.
First read-only search in a Region
creates an index and a default view.
Fallback drops tags from results.
3 · Two boxes, two answers.
Unified Search appends a wildcard
to the first keyword. The Resource
Explorer query box does not.
prod → matches / does not match
Someone will call it a deletion.
The audit
Who holds the read-only managed policy, or Search on *? Which Regions grew an index you never asked for?
Two mechanisms side by side, each correct on its own. The gap between them is where the assumption lives.
